author: Muhammad Hassan Siddiqui

hero.eyebrow: Measuring permission revocation in RAG over SharePoint
hero.question: You remove someone from a security group. How long can your copilot still show them the file?
hero.scope: One Microsoft 365 test tenant with synthetic documents. Azure AI Search measured in its basic ACL configuration.

findings.title: After an Entra-group removal, the three systems stop at very different times
findings.description: The same Entra security-group change was applied once and a removed user was read through three systems in one polling loop: SharePoint itself, Azure AI Search's SharePoint indexer in its basic ACL configuration, and a small revocation layer. For direct and SharePoint-group grants, SharePoint itself revoked quickly; the gap is specific to Entra-group changes.

findings.title: SharePoint groups in the basic ACL configuration
findings.description: In Azure AI Search's basic ACL configuration, documents granted to a SharePoint group were indexed with the group recorded but never served to its members. Microsoft documents an additional configuration for SharePoint-group support; it was not tested, so this is about the basic configuration only.

findings.title: In the agent tests, leaked content came from the shared cache and memory
findings.description: In the agent tests, the leaked content was delivered from the agent's shared cache and memory, not from retrieval; the counts show which path delivered each leak. A shared semantic cache and a shared long-term memory carry no permission information. Retrieval was not re-run on the cache-hit turns, so these tests do not show whether Azure AI Search would have returned the revoked document at that moment. A guarded agent re-checks every source of a cached answer for the current user on every hit and fails closed; the numbers show how it fared.

steps.title: Generate a test tenant
steps.description: A synthetic tenant is built from a spec: users, nested Entra groups, SharePoint groups, folders with unique permissions, and documents that each contain a unique canary string. Every run starts from a freshly generated tenant.

steps.title: Run the scenarios
steps.description: One permission change is applied and the same user is read through each system on a fixed interval until the system conforms or the cap is reached.
steps.code: uv run python -m leaklab.benchmark run --dir runs/benchmark_v2

steps.title: Score against the oracle
steps.description: An independent model of intended access, computed only from the spec and the confirmed changes, decides what the user should see. A leak is a canary served while intent denies it. Errors are never counted as denials; no language model judges anything.
steps.code: uv run python -m leaklab.benchmark report --dir runs/benchmark_v2

reproduce.heading: Reproduce it

tabs.label: Run
tabs.code:
uv run python -m leaklab.generator generate
uv run python -m leaklab.benchmark run --dir runs/benchmark_v2

tabs.label: Report
tabs.code:
uv run python -m leaklab.benchmark report --dir runs/benchmark_v2
uv run python -m leaklab.replay export --runs runs/benchmark_v2 --out optimus-main/public/replays

reproduce.note: Every script that writes to a tenant checks the tenant id against LEAKLAB_ALLOWED_TENANT_ID first.

systems_intro: Three systems, observed in the same polling loop, after the same permission change.
